# The Self-Growing DEX Frontier

> A way to build one AI from many departments without pooling their records. Each department grows a small specialist from its own records, on its own machine, from a signed seed of a few hundred bytes. A specialist that cannot prove itself on cases it never trained on is cut. The live ones answer together: each scores the case from what it knows, and a coupling learned from outcomes weighs their scores into one answer.

Live: https://sjgant80-hub.github.io/dex-frontier/
Code: https://github.com/sjgant80-hub/dex-frontier (MIT, no licence fee)

## Organs (sealed before measured; failures kept)
- Organ 1 · One specialist body: one department’s node against a 14B and a frontier model. 2 of 3 sealed rules held; the 7-column node 0.801 vs the 14B 0.741 and the frontier 0.844 on 300 customers.
- Organ 2 · The composition proof: specialists compose into more than the sum, before anything scales. 3 of 8 sealed rules held; composed 0.822 / 0.791 vs best node 0.813 / 0.810 vs every record pooled 0.846 / 0.827 (telecom / shop).
- Organ 2b · The composition fix: taken only if organ 2 finds composition does not net: nodes grown to complement. 3 of 5 sealed rules held; fixed mesh 0.813 / 0.818 vs best node 0.813 / 0.810.
- Organ 2c · The composition fix, third take: co-grown the way the mesh couples; every silo offers both its nodes. 1 of 4 sealed rules held; mesh 0.822 / 0.809 vs best node 0.813 / 0.810.
- Organ 2d · A nonlinear coupling: trees over the nodes’ scores learn interactions. 1 of 4 sealed rules held; mesh 0.817 / 0.830 vs best node 0.813 / 0.810; shop level with every record pooled (0.827).
- Organ 2e · The mesh chooses its coupling: linear or trees, chosen out of fold on GATE alone: the first of the gate’s three tests. 2 of 3 sealed rules held; linear / trees chosen; mesh 0.822 / 0.830 vs best node 0.813 / 0.810 — beyond the noise in both.
- Organ 2f · The gate retaken in full: all three of the gate’s tests at once, on two datasets no attempt had touched. 4 of 7 sealed rules held; mesh 0.786 / 0.896 vs best department 0.778 / 0.822 vs the frontier 0.820 / 0.937 (bank / census).
- Organ 2g · The gate taken again: all three tests on two more fresh datasets, the frontier test on 1,200 cases, growth beyond the noise. 1 of 7 sealed rules held; mesh 0.500 / 0.767 vs best department 0.500 / 0.748 vs the frontier 0.631 / 0.746 (hospital / credit).
- Organ 2h · The gate taken again, the join rule fixed: a department joins when it beats a coin beyond the noise; two more fresh datasets. 4 of 7 sealed rules held; mesh 0.729 / 0.840 vs best department 0.666 / 0.814 vs the frontier 0.738 / 0.823 (coupon / forest).
- Organ 3 · Breeding: a bred child beats both parents on cases neither saw; the population grows a better mesh. built and held until composition wins the gate; —.
- Organ 4 · Growing by working: each node sharpens as its records arrive. built and held until composition wins the gate; —.
- Organ 5 · The wisp: routing that learns from outcomes; a node gone bad is pruned. built and held until composition wins the gate; —.
- Organ 6 · Scale: cut finer, more nodes: the composed answer keeps climbing. built and held until composition wins the gate; —.
- Organ 7 · Sovereign spread: owned by contributors, carried by cards, revocable, scores only. built and held until composition wins the gate; —.

## Questions
- What is it? A way to build one AI from many departments without pooling their records. Each department grows a small specialist from its own records, on its own machine, from a signed seed of a few hundred bytes. A specialist that cannot prove itself on cases it never trained on is cut. The live ones answer together: each scores the case from what it knows, and a coupling learned from outcomes weighs their scores into one answer.
- Is this a large language model? No. What runs here answers questions about structured business records: will this customer leave, will this visitor buy. Each specialist is a handful of readable rules. The spec it was built from aims, in the end, at a distributed frontier language model grown the same way. What is proven here, on real data, is the step the spec says must come first: whether specialists compose into more than the sum.
- Do any records leave a department? No. A node reads only its own silo’s columns, on its own machine, and what crosses between nodes is a score per case. The page enforces the same in your browser: its security policy lets it connect only to its own site, and the data it uses are its own files.
- Did composition work? On two more datasets no attempt had touched, 3,805 coupon offers and 17,998 forest cells held out (organ 2h, a department joining when it beats a coin beyond the noise), the mesh scored 0.729 and 0.840. Beating its best department: held on the coupon offers (0.729 against 0.666, bound +0.050), held on the forest cells (0.840 against 0.814, bound +0.023). Approaching the frontier model on 1,200 cases: failed on the coupon offers (0.728 against 0.738, bound −0.032), held on the forest cells (0.834 against 0.823, bound −0.002). Growing measurably as departments join: held on the coupon offers (0.666 → 0.702 → 0.727 → 0.729, bound +0.050), held on the forest cells (0.814 → 0.827 → 0.835 → 0.839 → 0.840, bound +0.023). So the gate is not won, and by the spec nothing scales; every failed test is kept. Before it, organ 2g: On two more datasets no attempt had touched, 20,991 hospital stays and 8,999 credit clients held out (organ 2g, with 2f’s measurement faults fixed), the mesh scored 0.500 and 0.767. On the hospital stays every department was cut at its bar on its own (the best 0.580 against 0.6), so no mesh formed, while every record pooled scored 0.659: a bar that judges each department alone cut a signal spread thin across them. Beating its best department: failed on the hospital stays (no mesh), held on the credit clients (0.767 against 0.748, bound +0.010). Approaching the frontier model on 1,200 cases: failed on the hospital stays (no mesh), held on the credit clients (0.761 against 0.746, bound −0.007). Growing measurably as departments join: failed on the hospital stays (no mesh), held on the credit clients (0.748 → 0.760 → 0.767, bound +0.010). So the gate is not won, and by the spec nothing scales; every failed test is kept.
- How does it compare with putting every record in one place? On fresh cases, boosted trees with every record pooled in one place against the mesh, whose records never met: credit clients 0.780 against 0.767; bank calls 0.797 against 0.786; census people 0.912 against 0.896. Within 0.02 beyond the noise in all three. On the hospital stays every department was cut at its bar, so no mesh formed (pooled 0.659).
- How does it compare with a 14-billion-parameter model and a frontier model? On 1,200 fresh credit clients the frontier model, Claude Opus 5.5 asked cold, scored 0.746 and the mesh 0.761 on the same cases; on 1,200 hospital stays the frontier model scored 0.631 and every record pooled 0.659, where no mesh formed. In organ 2, on 300 cases per domain, both models saw every column and 24 past cases. The local qwen2.5:14b scored 0.741 (telecom) and 0.725 (shop). The frontier model, Claude Opus 5.5 asked cold, scored 0.844 and 0.858. Organ 2’s linear mesh scored 0.812 and 0.808 on the same cases. Beating the 14B did not hold in both domains; holding within 0.02 of the frontier model did not hold in both.
- How is this different from federated learning? Federated learning sends model updates, weights or gradients, from each party to a centre that averages them. Here each department’s records hold different columns about the same customers (the setting known as vertically partitioned data), and nothing is averaged. Each node is grown on its own columns, and what crosses is one score per case. The coupling is stacked generalisation, a known technique: a small model learns how to weigh the specialists’ answers.
- What if one department’s records are poor? Its node is cut. It must clear its bar on cases it never grew on, or it answers nothing and the rest carry on. On this page the shop’s context silo (browser, region, traffic source, visitor type) is that case: it was cut at its gate.
- Can a department leave, or join, without retraining everything? Yes. A node is unplugged by dropping it, and the coupling re-learns its few weights from held-back outcomes in milliseconds; no other node changes. Box 5 does it live. A new department grows its own node from its own seed and joins the same way.
- Can the nodes improve themselves? Two ways are built: breeding, where a child is born only if it beats both parents on cases neither grew on, and growing as records arrive. By the spec’s order, both are measured only once composition wins the gate, and it has not yet.
- What happens if a department’s node goes bad, or is taken over? The mesh is built to re-learn its coupling from outcomes and to prune a node that stops adding (organ 5). It is measured, with the strongest node broken half-way through a real stream, only once composition wins the gate.
- Does it keep working as more departments join? Organ 6 cuts the same records finer (7 and 6 silos) and adds the nodes one at a time. It is measured only once composition wins the gate.
- Who owns a node, and can they take it back? The contributor whose key sealed it. Organ 7 measures the rest: a node carried as a card, a ledger of each node’s share, and revoking a node without touching anyone else’s.
- What did not work? Every failed sealed prediction is kept on this page with its reason: organ 1’s A3, organ 2’s B2, organ 2’s B4, organ 2’s B5, organ 2’s B6, organ 2’s B7, organ 2b’s H2, organ 2b’s H4, organ 2c’s J2, organ 2c’s J3, organ 2c’s J4, organ 2d’s K2, organ 2d’s K3, organ 2d’s K4, organ 2e’s L3, organ 2f’s N3, organ 2f’s N4, organ 2f’s GATE, organ 2g’s P2, organ 2g’s P3, organ 2g’s P4, organ 2g’s P5, organ 2g’s P6, organ 2g’s GATE, organ 2h’s Q3, organ 2h’s Q5, organ 2h’s GATE. A failed property would turn the build red; a failed prediction is a finding.
- How do I check it myself? In this browser: box 2 grows all six nodes and checks them against CI’s record, and box 4 re-scores every test case. On your own machine, with Node 20 or later and the repository: npm test runs every test; node witness-all.mjs breaks every kernel line by line and checks the tests notice; node tools/measure-2.mjs --check re-derives the composition proof byte for byte. It takes someone who can run a command line.
- Can it see how one department’s columns interact with another’s? Partly, and this is the price of no record crossing. Each department sends one score per case, so a pattern that needs a column from billing and a column from the CRM together, seen raw, is invisible to both. What the mesh can do is weigh the departments’ scores against each other, and with the tree coupling it can learn that two scores together mean more than either alone. In the checks on held-back cases (FIT and GATE only), one boosted model per department, each sending one score, came within a hundredth of every record pooled on four of the six datasets and within two hundredths on all six: so on these data most of what pooling adds survives the one-score limit.
- Does it work in real time, and at scale? A node’s answer is a sum over a few dozen rules, so scoring a case takes a handful of comparisons, and the coupling a few more: fast enough to answer as each case arrives. Box 4 on this page re-scores every test case of both domains in your browser. Growing a node takes seconds to minutes per department on an ordinary machine. A new department grows one more node from its own seed, and the coupling re-learns; no other node changes.
- What does a pilot take? One question whose answer lives across two or three departments, and a few people’s time: someone in each department runs the seal and the grow on their own machine, and someone joins the departments’ scores on a held-back slice of past cases, keyed by a case id they share, to learn the coupling. Then it runs beside your current process while you compare its calls with what happened. The code carries no licence fee; support is agreed per deployment with AI Native Solutions.
- What does it cost? The code is MIT licensed: no licence fee. It runs on machines you already have, with no cloud, no model hosting and no central data store. Support is agreed per deployment with AI Native Solutions.
